question: Bound employers can fill some full-time posts with more workers each averaging under 30 hours.
rationale: K1 applies only to employees averaging 30 or more hours, and employees under 30 hours are expressly exempt. Splitting a full-time post into part-time posts therefore removes the offer obligation or the $3,000 charge. Part-timers still count toward the FTE threshold by their hours, but that does not matter for a firm already bound. The uncovered full-timers are concentrated in retail, food service, cleaning, security and care, where shift-based work is commonly divided among part-timers. That makes such substitution feasible for at least some posts. The closest assumption is A-10 (rescheduling 30–35-hour jobs to under 30 at a cost below the per-head cost, p 0.75), which supports this. The question asks only whether some posts can be filled this way, which is a weaker claim. Limits include training and turnover costs and imperfect substitutability of hours (A-11, 0.65). Even so, 'some' is a low bar.

premises: Bound employers can fill some full-time posts with more workers each averaging under 30 hours.
proposal.source: Exemptions: Public employers. Employees averaging under 30 hours.

question: Bound employers can contract out cleaning, security or food service to independent firms under 50 FTE.
rationale: The Act does not bar contracting out. K3 combines only firms under common control, and workers supplied by an agency count for the agency, not the client. A cleaning, security or food-service contractor that is independent and under 50 FTE is therefore unbound, and its workers are not counted toward the client's FTE. Such services are routinely contracted out. The record is otherwise silent on outsourcing. A-17 (p 0.55) is narrower: it concerns firms near 50 doing so at a cost below the term or charge. This question asks only whether the route is open, so I judge from the text. Doubts remain over whether small contractors exist at scale and whether Revenue might treat sham arrangements as common control.

premises: Bound employers can contract out cleaning, security or food service to independent firms under 50 FTE.
proposal.source: Firms under common control are counted together. Agency workers count for the agency.

question: Some bound employers near Marisport can move work across the border to Tarnley.
rationale: The record does not say directly whether bound firms can relocate work. It does say that Marisport lies on the Tarnley border, that Tarnley has no such law, and that about 35,000 people cross daily, so labour markets are integrated. The claim is weak: it only requires that some bound employers can move some work. Bound firms include national chains, staffing and security firms and possibly food processors with tradable output, and some of them plausibly can shift operations or hiring a few miles across the border. A-26 (tradable producers compete with Tarnley, p 0.65) is related but not the same statement. Location-bound local services (retail, food service, care) mostly cannot move, which keeps p below 0.85.

question: Bound retail and food firms pass part of higher labour costs into their prices.
rationale: The record does not state pass-through directly. Some pass-through is plausible: the per-head cost raises marginal cost for bound mid-size, low-wage firms, and minimum-wage binding (A-9) limits how much can be shifted onto wages. Higher prices can follow as marginal output or entry shrinks. Several factors limit it. Unbound competitors (small, already-compliant and capped firms, A-22 at 0.65) compete in the same local product markets. It is doubtful that most competitors bear a material per-head cost (A-24 at 0.4). The capped chains bear only about $200 per head. Tarnley firms near the Marisport border add competition. Part of the cost also falls on wages over time (A-6, A-8). So pass-through is likely to be partial and uneven, which leans yes but not strongly.

question: Many bound chains compete mainly with other bound chains facing the same cost.
rationale: No assumption row matches exactly. A-24, the closest, concerns mid-size bound firms rather than chains, and puts at 0.4 the chance that most of their local competitors bear a material per-head cost. Chains do largely compete with other chains, and all chains have 50+ FTE, so all are bound. But the record shows the Act's cost is very uneven among them. Most large firms already offer compliant cover, so their added cost is about nil. The 45 non-offering chains are capped at about $200 per head. Mid-size payers face $3,000 per head. Chains also compete with unbound small firms and with Tarnley stores at the Marisport border. So 'facing the same cost' holds only for some chains, and 'many' does not clearly hold. The answer leans no, near A-24's p.

question: Bound firms that choose to offer buy qualifying group plans from insurers.
rationale: The record does not say how players obtain cover. Under K1, a bound firm that offers must provide a plan meeting K2. K2 applies to insurers and self-insured employers, so self-insurance is also allowed. Most firms that would newly offer, and most firms upgrading short plans, are mid-size, with roughly 36 uncovered full-timers each. Firms of that size usually buy fully insured group plans because self-insuring at that scale is costly and risky. Large firms may self-insure, but even they usually buy stop-loss cover and administration from insurers. Assumption A-2 (p 0.75) says some bound firms that offer nothing now will choose to offer. If they offer, buying insured group plans is the main channel. The probability is somewhat below certainty because of the self-insurance route and because A-2 itself is uncertain.

question: Bound employers can cut training, scheduling flexibility and other non-money terms where wages cannot fall.
rationale: No row in the assumption table states this, so I judged it from the record and general knowledge. The record says R1 sets a $14.00 floor on money wages. It says nothing about training, scheduling or other non-wage terms, so those are left unregulated. A-9 holds that the minimum wage binds for some workers at bound firms. A-3 holds that money wages are sticky in the short run. Where the wage cannot fall, employers bearing the $5,180 term or the $3,000 charge can still adjust unregulated terms such as training, scheduling flexibility, perks and work intensity. This is a standard, well-known margin of adjustment under minimum wages and mandates. The record does not show whether every bound employer can do this, and some terms may be fixed by contracts or other law. The general capacity is highly plausible, so the answer is yes.

question: Where the minimum wage holds the wage, bound employers face more applicants than full-time posts.
rationale: Where R1 binds, the wage cannot fall to absorb the K1 cost. That cost is $2.49 an hour per full-timer at 40 hours for players, or $1.44 for payers. Bound employers therefore want fewer full-time posts at the floor wage. The binding floor already implies more people willing to work at that wage than posts on offer. At players, the added cover also makes the posts more attractive. Both effects widen the gap between applicants and full-time posts. The answer rests on the minimum wage binding at some bound firms (A-9, 0.85) and on workers' alternatives being only partial (A-37). Some workers may leave for unbound work or Tarnley, which keeps the probability a little below A-9's p. The record does not report applicant numbers directly.

question: An employee who is offered cover and declines costs the employer nothing under K1.
rationale: K1 says an employee who is offered cover and declines counts as offered. So no $250-a-month charge is owed for that employee. If the employee declines, the employer also pays no premium contribution. Under K1 itself, a declined offer therefore costs the employer nothing. The only remaining costs are minor ones outside K1's charge: arranging a certified plan and reporting offer status on quarterly returns under K5. That leaves a little doubt about the literal 'nothing'.

question: Some bound employers can reclassify employees as independent contractors outside K1.

K1 and K3 apply only to employees, and the agency-worker rule closes only the staffing route. Reclassification was generally known at enactment to be feasible in some of the affected sectors: cleaning, security, landscaping and some care work. Its legality depends on the state's employment-status tests, which the record does not give. Because the claim needs only some bound employers to be able to do this, at some legal and enforcement risk, it is moderately likely true.

question: The per-head cost of K1 is large relative to pay at bound firms that offer nothing.
rationale: No assumption row states this directly, so the answer rests on the policy record. The record gives the cost of the 70% employer share as $5,180 a year, which is 17.8% of a full-time minimum-wage worker's pay. That works out to $2.49 an hour at 40 hours a week and $3.32 at 30. Even the cheaper option, the penalty, is $1.44 to $1.92 an hour, roughly 10 to 14% of the $14.00 minimum wage. The firms that offer nothing are mostly low-wage retail, food service, security and staffing. So for uncapped firms the per-head cost is large relative to pay. The main exception is the capped firms, where the cap works out to only $200 per head. That exception, plus some higher-wage non-offering firms, lowers the probability somewhat.

question: Profits of bound firms are paid to their owners.
rationale: The record does not say how bound firms' profits are distributed. The assumption table has no matching row. Bound firms are private employers: national retail and food chains, staffing and security firms, and mid-size private firms. By the ordinary residual-claimant structure of private firms, their profits accrue to owners (shareholders, proprietors), whether paid out or retained, and retained profit raises owners' equity. The Act does not take or redirect profits. It imposes a per-head charge, capped at $300,000, which reduces profit rather than changing who receives it. The only doubt is literal: some profit is retained rather than paid out, and some bound firms may be cooperatives or nonprofits, which have no owners to pay.

question: The cap cuts the charge per uncovered head far below $3,000 for firms with many uncovered full-timers.
rationale: The record answers this directly. K4 caps the charge at $300,000 a year, a ceiling reached at 100 uncovered employees. Past that point the charge per uncovered head falls as $300,000 divided by the head count. The record's own example is a firm with 1,500 uncovered full-timers, which pays $200 per head instead of $3,000. The 45 large firms have more than 100 such employees each, and A-12 (p 0.9) says they stay above 100, so the statement holds for firms with many uncovered full-timers. The only uncertainty is how to read "far below" for firms just over 100 uncovered heads.

question: Above 100 uncovered full-timers the capped charge does not change with hiring or wages.
rationale: Under K4 the charge is capped at $300,000 a year, and the cap is reached at 100 uncovered employees. K1 sets the charge as a flat $250 a month per uncovered employee, with no link to wages. So once a firm has more than 100 uncovered full-timers, hiring another one, or raising or cutting wages, leaves the charge at $300,000. At the margin the charge is zero. The only way it changes is if the firm falls to 100 or fewer uncovered full-timers. A-12 puts the chance that capped firms stay above that line at 0.9, but the question is conditional on being above 100. No assumption row states this exact claim, so the answer rests on the statutory text.

question: Capped chains can move outlets to franchisees not under their common control.
rationale: The record does not say how franchisees are treated. K3 counts firms under common control together, and franchising is a common, established way for retail and food chains to restructure. Since the record is silent, the default is that independently owned franchisees are not under the franchisor's common control, so the move looks legally and practically open, though it takes time and money. A-17 speaks only of firms near 50 FTE, not capped chains, so it is not the same statement; it does lend some support (p 0.55). Whether capped chains would want to franchise is a separate question. At the cap the marginal charge is zero, so splitting into separate franchisees could raise total liability. That bears on incentive, not on whether the option exists. Staffing and security firms are less able to franchise, which lowers confidence.

question: Seasonal firms can hire their seasonal workers through staffing agencies or labour contractors.
rationale: The record allows this route. K3 says agency workers count for the agency, so seasonal hours supplied through an agency or contractor would not count toward the seasonal firm's own 50-FTE total. The record does not say whether the 380 seasonal firms actually have access to such intermediaries. It was well known at enactment that farms, food processors, resorts and landscapers often use farm labour contractors and staffing agencies for seasonal crews. That makes the option plausibly open to many of them. Some cost and availability doubt remains, which A-17 (0.55) reflects for contracting out generally. question: Seasonal firms can keep seasonal workers' hours or stints short enough to avoid owing an offer.
rationale: An offer is owed only to an employee averaging 30 or more hours (130 a month) at a bound firm, from the first of the month after 60 days of employment. A seasonal firm can therefore avoid owing an offer by keeping stints under about 60 days or hours under 30, and both are mechanically open. The question asks about feasibility, which is broader than A-30's claim that employers actually shorten engagements (p 0.4). Many seasons (ski, lake, harvest) run 90–120 days, so cutting stints below 60 days means rotating crews, with extra hiring and training costs. Capping hours under 30 conflicts with peak-season demand and with overtime-free scheduling. So some seasonal firms, not all, can do this at an acceptable cost. The record is silent on how costly this is in practice.

question: Hours of an employee averaging 130 or more hours a month add nothing to the firm's FTE count.
rationale: Under K3, an employee averaging 130 or more hours a month counts as exactly one FTE, as a head. Only other employees' hours are converted, at hours ÷ 130. So once an employee is at or above 130 hours, extra hours do not raise the FTE count. This is why lengthening full-timers' hours can substitute for adding heads near the threshold. The employee still counts as one head, so the 'yes' depends on reading the question as asking whether that employee's hours themselves add to the count, rather than whether the employee does.

question: Firms near 50 FTE can lengthen existing full-timers' hours, paying overtime, instead of hiring.
rationale: Under K3, an employee averaging 130 or more hours a month counts as exactly one FTE, however many hours they work. So adding hours for existing full-timers does not raise a firm's FTE count, while hiring a new full-timer adds one. R4 permits hours above 40 at 1.5 times the regular rate, so the option is legally open; its cost is the overtime premium. No assumption row matches exactly. A-11 (p 0.65) covers substituting extra hours for heads between 30 and 40 hours, not overtime above 40. A-14 says some firms near 50 value staying below the line more than the extra work. For at least some firms near the threshold, longer hours plausibly substitute for new heads, though limits on fatigue and output cap this. The record is silent on how widely this happens; 'can' asks only whether it is feasible for some firms, which favours yes.

question: Crossing 50 FTE would raise a firm's labour costs by up to $3,000 per uncovered full-timer.
rationale: Under K1, a firm at or above 50 FTE must either offer qualifying cover (70% share = $5,180/yr) or pay $3,000 a year for each full-timer not offered. Because the firm can always choose the charge, the direct cost of each uncovered full-timer is capped at $3,000. The K4 cap ($300,000) only lowers this further and does not apply to firms near 50. A firm would offer cover only if that were worth it to it (for example, offset by wage adjustment or by workers valuing cover). So the statutory increase is at most $3,000 per uncovered full-timer. One minor caveat: reporting and compliance costs under K5 come on top, which is why confidence is not higher.

question: Insurers pass the cost of meeting and certifying plans under K2 into the premiums they charge employers.
rationale: No assumption row states this directly, so it is judged from the record. Plans that fall short of K2 on benefits or deductible must add hospital, physician, prescription and maternity cover with a deductible of at most $2,500. That raises expected claims, and insurers set premiums on expected claims plus administration, so the cost of meeting the standard mostly shows up in the premium for a compliant plan. The record already prices a standard-meeting employee-only plan at $7,400. Certification is done by the Department of Insurance, funded from the general fund. The record names no certification fee, so any certification cost to insurers is likely small (paperwork), but it too would normally be priced in. The main uncertainties are how competitive the insurance market is, and that for the 79% already offered compliant plans there is no extra cost to pass on. Both bear on how much is passed through, not on its direction, so the answer leans yes.

question: Several insurers compete for employer group plans in Quenby, so cost changes reach premiums at renewal.
rationale: The record says nothing about the structure of Quenby's group insurance market, and no assumption row states this claim. question: Many full-timers newly offered cover at bound firms earn below 200% of the poverty line.

A full-time minimum-wage worker earns $29,120, and workers paid somewhat above the minimum also fall below 200% FPL, especially those with dependents. The uncovered full-timers are concentrated in low-wage retail, food service, security and care, and many work at mid-size firms. Two things pull against a confident yes. Low-wage firms are likelier to pay the charge than to offer (A-2, A-4), so the newly offered skew toward higher-paid staff. The capped chains, which employ many of the lowest-paid, will mostly pay. Still, firms that upgrade short plans (A-5) and some low-wage players likely put many sub-200% FPL workers among the newly offered. The closest assumption row is A-28 (p 0.7). The mechanism itself follows almost directly from the ICP's eligibility rule. Status for 2028 is set by the 2027 average, and the Act was signed on 4 January 2027, so most 2027 seasonal hiring (summer farms, lake resorts, landscaping, processing) was still ahead and could be reduced. question: Profits of physician practices, pharmacies and for-profit hospitals are paid to their owners.
rationale: The record does not address who receives provider profits, so the answer rests on general knowledge. By definition, the residual earnings of physician practices, pharmacies and for-profit hospitals belong to their owners: partners, proprietors or shareholders. They are paid out as distributions or dividends, or kept as retained equity value. The record contains nothing that redirects these profits, such as a profit cap or tax. This matters because extra care billed to insurers (A-27) raises provider revenue, and any profit from that accrues to owners. Some profit is retained rather than paid out, but it still belongs to the owners, so the claim holds in substance.

question: Hospitals, physicians and pharmacies need more nursing and support staff hours to provide more care.

question: Longer hours worked by existing staff at firms near 50 FTE let those firms produce more than they otherwise would.
rationale: Under K3, an employee averaging 130 or more hours a month counts as exactly 1 FTE no matter how many further hours they work. Hours above 40 cost 1.5 times the regular rate under R4, but this still lets the firm produce more than it could with its headcount held below 50 and hours unchanged. But misclassification of workers who stay under the firm's control carries legal risk, and K5's quarterly reporting with a double penalty for misreporting adds more. question: Some people who take added jobs at firms under 50 FTE were not in paid work before.
rationale: The record does not address who fills added jobs at small firms. A-22 says unbound firms compete with mid-size bound firms in local product markets, and A-14 says some firms near 50 FTE prefer to stay under the line. Small, unbound firms are likely to gain some share and add jobs. Some of those hires would plausibly be people entering from non-employment: students, the unemployed, people returning to work. Quenby's labor force is large and turnover is normal, so 'some' is a weak claim. The main doubt is whether small firms add jobs on net at all. Workers moving across from bound firms (A-8) could also fill most of the posts. On balance, likely yes.

question: Workers who take paid jobs have less time for producing goods and care at home.
rationale: The record does not address this directly, and no row in the assumption table states it. It is a general fact about how time is used: hours spent in paid work cannot also be spent producing goods or giving care at home. So a worker who takes a paid job, or works more paid hours, gives up home production time, all else equal. Possible exceptions, such as someone who replaces leisure rather than home work, or who buys substitutes, do not change the core claim that available time is reduced.

question: Tarnley employers near Marisport hire fewer workers when the wages they must pay rise.
rationale: The record does not address Tarnley employers' labor demand directly. The question states a general law-of-demand proposition: other things equal, a higher wage cost leads employers to hire fewer workers. Nothing in the record suggests that Tarnley employers near the border are an exception. They are not bound by the Act, and Tarnley is named as an alternative for Quenby workers and as a competitor of Quenby producers. That role as an alternative depends on Tarnley hiring responding to wages: if Quenby workers' moving lowers the wage Tarnley employers must pay, they hire more, and conversely. Monopsony could weaken this at the margin, so the probability is high but not certain.
